text: Every query you've written in this course so far, unless you explicitly said otherwise, ran under READ COMMITTED -- it's SQL Server's default isolation level for every new connection. No SET statement needed.

READ COMMITTED guarantees exactly what its name says: every read only ever sees committed data. Go back to the dirty-read timeline from a few lessons ago -- under READ COMMITTED, that second session's read would simply block, waiting for the first transaction's exclusive lock to release, instead of reading the in-flight value.

But READ COMMITTED does not hold its shared locks for the whole transaction -- only for as long as each individual statement's read takes. The moment that one SELECT finishes, the lock releases, even if the surrounding transaction is still open. That's exactly the gap that let the nonrepeatable read and the phantom read slip through in the last two lessons.

You can check exactly what level a session is running under with DBCC USEROPTIONS -- look for the isolation level row in the result. It's easy to forget you changed this earlier in a session, so it's worth verifying when something feels off.
So READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads, and only dirty reads. Nonrepeatable reads and phantom reads are both still on the table, because of how briefly its locks are actually held.

Next lesson, we move one notch stricter: REPEATABLE READ, the level where nonrepeatable reads finally stop being possible -- by holding its locks for the whole transaction instead of releasing them early. See you there.
